mapped_modules.rationale: AIPE's f.calculus module is defined in the taxonomy as slopes, areas, exponentials and first-order differential equations introduced through charging and discharging circuits. Those four ideas are exactly the spine of this course (Units 1-3 plus the separable-ODE Sessions 39-40), so the course is the central academic reference for the module. The course goes far beyond the AIPE module in breadth (techniques of integration, series, polar coordinates) and never uses circuits as motivation; AIPE's module is a circuit-motivated subset of it. Taylor series (Session 98) is deliberately not listed here: it is a proposed extension of f.calculus (see the Taylor-series recommended lesson), not current module content, and appears under pe.modelling as background.

AIPE f.computation covers scripts, plots and simulation models with numerical integration, step sizes and numerical error. The course treats numerical integration in two sessions (the Session 63 page lists clips titled Introduction to Numerical Integration, Riemann Sums, Trapezoidal Rule and Simpson's Rule, plus a Riemann Sums mathlet) and root finding in one session on Newton's method, as hand methods rather than scripts. This is a brief, theory-side treatment of what AIPE teaches computationally, hence introductory. Newton's method (Session 33) is proposed as a root-finding addition to f.computation; the current module summary lists numerical integration only.

courses.coverage_notes: MIT 18.01SC (OCW Scholar edition, Fall 2010, Prof. David Jerison) is a self-contained single-variable calculus course for independent learners. It runs through five units: differentiation (definition, rules, implicit differentiation, exponentials and inverses), applications of differentiation (approximation, curve sketching, optimization, related rates, Newton's method, Mean Value Theorem, antiderivatives and a first look at separable differential equations), the definite integral and its applications (Riemann sums, both Fundamental Theorems, areas, volumes, averages, probability, numerical integration), techniques of integration (trigonometric methods, partial fractions, integration by parts, arc length, parametric and polar curves), and infinite processes (L'Hospital's rule, improper integrals, series and Taylor series). The material is organised as 102 sequential sessions (Sessions 1-101 on the five unit pages, Session 102 on the final-exam page); most sessions pair segmented lecture-video clips with notes and a worked example, many add recitation videos or an interactive mathlet, each part ends with a problem set and each unit with an exam. Positioning stated in the syllabus: a first-year, first-semester MIT subject with an estimated total effort of about 150 hours; no textbook is required, the course being described as self-contained, with any single-variable calculus text usable as an optional companion.
gaps: Complex numbers and Euler's formula as the bridge from Taylor series to phasors: absent from the 18.01SC outline (Unit 5 Part B lists no complex-number item). Complex arithmetic and sinusoidal functions appear in the Unit I navigation of the 18.03SC home page (baseline record mit-18-03sc-2011), so this is a gap of this course, not of the baseline.

Second-order linear differential equations with constant coefficients (RLC response, resonance, damping): 18.01SC stops at separable first-order equations; the 18.03SC home page lists Unit II 'Second Order Constant Coefficient Linear Equations' with damped oscillators and resonance (mit-18-03sc-2011).

Laplace transforms, transfer functions and poles, which AIPE f.signals needs directly: not in 18.01SC; listed in 18.03SC Unit III and in the 6.003 syllabus description (mit-18-03sc-2011, mit-6-003-2011).

Fourier series and harmonic content of periodic waveforms: 18.01SC integrates trigonometric powers but never introduces orthogonality or Fourier coefficients; Fourier series are listed in 18.03SC Unit III and Fourier representations in the 6.003 syllabus (mit-18-03sc-2011, mit-6-003-2011).

Numerical solution of differential equations: none in 18.01SC; the 18.03SC home page lists a 'Numerical Methods' session in Unit I (mit-18-03sc-2011) whose method names were not read for this record. RK4, step-size and stiffness choices and energy-conservation checks, which pe.simulation and f.computation rely on, remain a baseline-wide AIPE gap; AIPE's buck-converter-fundamentals lab already uses fixed-step first-order (semi-implicit Euler) integration without a lesson that teaches the method.

Discrete-time calculus: sampling, difference equations and discrete integrators for digital control: not in 18.01SC; the 6.003 syllabus names discrete-time signals, sampling and difference equations (mit-6-003-2011).

Calculus on piecewise and switched waveforms (averaging over a switching period, volt-second and charge balance, small-ripple approximation): not in 18.01SC; assigned in the catalogue to the 6.622 baseline record (mit-6-622-2023). The 6.622 home and syllabus pages read for this record do not name these topics, so the pointer is catalogue organisation to be evidenced in that record.

Multivariable calculus (partial derivatives, gradients and constrained optimisation for loss models, MPPT and design trade-offs): not in 18.01SC; the 18.02SC syllabus lists partial derivatives, gradient and directional derivatives, and Lagrange multipliers (mit-18-02sc-2010).

Vector calculus and the integral forms of Maxwell's equations needed by f.electromagnetism and f.magnetism: not in 18.01SC; assigned in the catalogue to the 8.02 and 6.013 records (mit-8-02-2007, mit-6-013-2005). The 8.02 home page and the 6.013 syllabus read for this record do not list these topics by name (6.013 names Maxwell's equations only as a prerequisite), so the pointer is catalogue organisation.
Computational tooling (Python/NumPy/SymPy) for symbolic and numeric calculus: the course's interactive tools are legacy Java mathlets; a baseline-wide AIPE gap.

Energy-domain applications: integrating power to energy (W to Wh), average and RMS of electrical waveforms, and small-ripple estimates in a circuit context: not framed this way in 18.01SC, so AIPE lessons must supply the circuit framing themselves; a baseline-wide AIPE gap.

courses.coverage_notes: 18.02SC is the OCW Scholar (self-study) edition of MIT's second-semester freshman calculus, taught by Prof. Denis Auroux: vector and matrix algebra, calculus of functions of several variables (partial derivatives, gradient, chain rule, optimisation with and without constraints), double and triple integrals in several coordinate systems, and vector calculus in two and three dimensions culminating in Green's, Stokes' and the divergence theorems, with a short physics-applications coda on Maxwell's equations. It is organised into 4 units, 12 parts and 102 numbered sessions, of which Sessions 22-23, 45-46 and 73 are unit-exam reviews and Sessions 99-102 are final-exam reviews. A typical session (Session 1 sampled) links a segmented lecture-video clip (recorded fall 2007) with board images, lecture notes, worked examples, a recitation video and problems with solutions; the syllabus says most sessions include lecture clips and some include Mathlets. The course has 12 problem sets (one per part), 4 unit exams and a final exam; solutions are linked on every sampled problem-set and exam page and Problem Set Solutions / Exam Solutions are listed resource types. The syllabus describes the course as self-contained with no required textbook and estimates roughly 150 hours of study.
gaps: Numerical multivariable methods used in power engineering: Newton-Raphson for nonlinear systems (power flow), numerical Jacobians, quadrature for multiple integrals, finite-difference solution of the diffusion equation; the course is analytic and provides no code

Linear algebra beyond 3x3 systems: eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalisation, matrix exponential and state-space models needed by pe.modelling, f.signals and ps.stability; Unit 1 stops at inverses of square systems

Complex numbers and phasors (f.ac), Laplace and Fourier transforms (f.signals) and ordinary differential equations for RC/RL/RLC dynamics (f.dynamics); 18.02SC assumes 18.01 and leaves ordinary differential equations to 18.03SC: although OCW tags the course with Differential Equations, its only differential-equation session is Session 87 (Diffusion Equation), a partial differential equation

Least squares in matrix/regression form and optimisation algorithms (gradient descent, KKT conditions, convex programming) used for parameter extraction, MPPT, economic dispatch and energy management; the course gives only the calculus statements

Engineering-contextualised field applications: Ampere's law and flux for inductor and transformer magnetics design, Gauss's law for cable and coaxial geometries, heat conduction in power devices; the course's applications are mass, moment of inertia, gravitation and generic Maxwell equations
Reproducible open-source computation (Python/NumPy/SciPy/Matplotlib, ngspice) in place of the 2010 Java-applet Mathlets for visualising surfaces, contours, vector fields and flux

mit_topics: First Order Constant Coefficient Linear ODE's

mapped_modules.rationale: AIPE's f.calculus module pairs calculus (slopes, areas, exponentials) with first-order differential equations introduced through charging and discharging circuits. MIT Unit I is a deep, twelve-session treatment of the ODE half (separable and linear equations, integrating factors, direction fields, autonomous equations, stability of critical points), while the calculus half is assumed as the 18.01 prerequisite and not taught. The label is 'partial' for the module as a whole, consistent with the f.ac rating below; for the first-order-ODE half alone the coverage would be core.

mit_topics: Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag
Step and Delta Functions: Integrals and Generalized Derivatives
Unit Step and Unit Impulse Response
mapped_modules.rationale: The module summary (LTI systems, step and frequency response, Laplace transforms, poles, Bode plots, negative feedback) is the central subject matter of Units II and III: LTI operators, amplitude and phase response, step and impulse response, convolution, Laplace-transform solution of initial value problems, transfer and weight functions and pole diagrams. The exponential response formula (Exponential Response, Undetermined Coefficients) is the transfer function evaluated at the input exponent, which the Poles, Amplitude Response, Connection to ERF session builds on, and the three Fourier-series sessions handle periodic input by superposition over Fourier components. The course lists a note on Bode plots (Amplitude Phase, Gain and Bode Plots, on the Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag page) but nothing on negative feedback, loop shaping or gain and phase margins, so one module item is not covered. The home-page navigation lists all the sessions named here; per-session URLs are in topic_outline.

mit_topics: First Order Constant Coefficient Linear ODE's
Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag
mapped_modules.rationale: The mathematics of RC/RL responses and time constants (first-order constant-coefficient linear ODEs with step, exponential and sinusoidal inputs) and of RLC ringing (damped harmonic oscillator, damping ratio) is central to the course, but the module's physical content, capacitors and inductors as energy-storage elements, appears only in the single Applications: LRC Circuits session (notes titled RLC Circuits and Impedance plus a Series RLC Circuits Applet note); the syllabus goals otherwise name driven spring-mass systems as the physical model, so coverage is substantial but not central.

mit_topics: Matrix Methods: Eigenvalues and Normal Modes
mapped_modules.rationale: Unit IV treats 2x2 constant-coefficient linear systems x' = Ax, i.e. the state-space description named in the module summary, with eigenvalues and eigenvectors, normal modes, fundamental matrices and the matrix exponential; the Linear Systems session page lists a note titled Review of Vectors and Matrices (also on the lecture-notes listing) and notes on matrix notation and the companion matrix. It is one unit of four and limited to 2x2 systems, and the module's node-equation and large-system solving content is not taught, so coverage is partial.

mit_topics: Exponential Input; Gain and Phase Lag
mapped_modules.rationale: Complex numbers, Euler's formula and the complex-exponential (phasor-style) method for sinusoidal inputs, amplitude-phase form, gain and phase lag, and the note titled Impedance on the Applications: LRC Circuits page cover the complex-number half of the module in depth. Period, frequency, duty cycle, average and RMS values and AC power are not listed anywhere in the course, so coverage is partial rather than core.

The Numerical Methods session page lists an introduction note, notes titled Motivation and Implementation of Euler's Method, Errors in Euler's Method and Further Numerical Methods, video resource pages titled Euler's Method, Example of Euler's Method, Better Methods and Pitfalls, an Euler's Method Applet note with an exploration page, a worked exercise, a recitation video and the usual practice-problem and problem-set files; the syllabus course goals also name Euler's method and direction fields. So Euler's method, its error and the existence of better methods are taught in one session. Programming, plotting and simulation-model building are not taught, and step-size and error discussion is confined to this session, so the treatment is introductory relative to the module summary.

courses.coverage_notes: 18.03SC is the OCW Scholar self-study edition of MIT's undergraduate differential-equations course. It is built from four units: first-order ODEs (analytic, geometric and numerical methods, complex arithmetic, sinusoidal and exponential inputs, autonomous equations), second-order constant-coefficient linear equations (characteristic equation, damped oscillators, exponential response, gain and phase lag, resonance, frequency response, an LRC-circuit application), Fourier series and Laplace transform (periodic input, step and delta functions, impulse response, convolution, transfer functions, poles), and first-order 2x2 systems (matrix methods, eigenvalues, phase portraits, matrix exponentials, linearisation of nonlinear systems, limit cycles and chaos). The navigation lists 39 session pages plus three unit exams and a final. Most session pages link course-note PDFs, clips from Prof. Mattuck's lectures, recitation videos, Mathlet pages, practice problems and two-part problem sets with solutions; the Conventions and Preliminary Material, Linear vs. Nonlinear and Applications: LRC Circuits sessions carry no video links. The syllabus overview frames the course around linear ODEs and the ways scientists and engineers use them, and states that MIT students put about 150 hours into it across 38 sessions.
gaps: Practical numerical ODE solving as engineers use it: adaptive step size, implicit and stiff solvers, the scipy.integrate.solve_ivp workflow and the stiffness of switching-converter models. (The Numerical Methods session page lists Errors in Euler's Method, a Better Methods video page and Further Numerical Methods, so higher-order fixed-step methods are at least named by the course.)
Gain and phase margins, loop shaping and negative-feedback design on Bode plots (the course lists a Bode-plot note, amplitude/phase response and pole diagrams, but no feedback loops).
Discrete-time dynamics: sampled systems, difference equations, z-transform and digital control implementation needed by pe.control.
Switched and piecewise-linear systems, state-space averaging and small-signal models of converters (the course treats continuous LTI systems only).
State-space modelling above 2x2 order and numerical eigenvalue analysis of large systems, as needed for converter-dominated grid stability studies.
Fourier transform, DFT/FFT, harmonic spectra and total harmonic distortion for measured waveforms (the course covers Fourier series only).
Phasor-domain AC power quantities: RMS and average values, real/reactive/apparent power, three-phase phasors.
Open computational tooling for verification: Python/NumPy/SciPy scripts and ngspice circuit simulation compared against hand analysis (the course relies on Java Mathlets).
Electromechanical dynamics (swing equation), frequency dynamics and small-signal stability in inverter-dominated grids as applications of the ODE theory.

Whether the non-PDF resource pages linked from session pages (e.g. Euler's Method, Better Methods, Pitfalls) are lecture clips or recitation videos was not confirmed; they are recorded as video resource pages.

The syllabus text refers to 38 sessions while the navigation lists 39 session pages (the first is Conventions and Preliminary Material, whose lecture-note filenames carry session number s0); both figures are recorded as read, without reconciling them.

Within-session note titles were recorded only where cited in rationales (Amplitude Phase, Gain and Bode Plots; RLC Circuits; Impedance; Review of Vectors and Matrices; the Numerical Methods session's Euler's-method resources); the topic outline otherwise stops at session level.
concepts_missing_in_aipe: First-order ODE theory beyond what the module summaries name: separable equations, integrating factors, existence and uniqueness, and superposition for linear equations. First-order differential equations are named generically in the f.calculus and f.dynamics summaries, but these techniques are not named and curriculum/catalogue.json attaches no lesson or lab to either module.
Geometric methods: direction fields and isoclines for first-order ODEs (named in no module summary and in no repository file).

Euler's method and its error as an explicitly taught foundations topic. The f.computation summary names numerical integration, step sizes and numerical error; the only implementation is the fixed-step semi-implicit Euler scheme inside labs/power-electronics/buck_switching.py, whose docstring documents its step-dependent error and which the buck fundamentals lesson (curriculum/power-electronics/dc-dc-conversion/buck-converter-fundamentals.md) describes in its lab-method paragraph. No lesson teaches the method, its error order or its step-size limits, and catalogue.json attaches nothing to f.computation.
First-order autonomous equations: phase lines, critical points and their stability; linear versus nonlinear behaviour (named in no module summary and in no repository file).

Second-order constant-coefficient theory: characteristic equation and modes, under-, critically and over-damped responses. The term damping ratio appears only in the buck fundamentals lesson, where zeta = sqrt(L/C)/(2R) is applied to the start-up transient of the output filter; no foundations lesson develops the general second-order theory.
Exponential response formula, undetermined coefficients and the amplitude-phase form of sinusoidal responses (named in no module summary; f.ac and f.signals have no lesson).

Pure versus practical resonance of a driven second-order system as general theory. LC resonance appears only applied to the buck output filter in the draft tutorial curriculum/03-converters/buck-converter.md (natural frequency, Q and the resonant peak of the duty-to-output transfer function) and in the buck fundamentals lesson's start-up transient; resonant converters are mentioned in the stage-03 outline; pe.resonant has no lesson.

Fourier series of periodic inputs, operations on Fourier series and the response of an LTI system to periodic input by superposition. No module summary names Fourier series, although pe.rectifiers and pe.inverters name harmonics; 'Fourier' appears in no repository file in English or Chinese.

Delta functions and generalised derivatives, the unit impulse response, the convolution integral and Green's formula. Step response is named in the f.signals summary, but these items appear in no module summary and in no repository file.

Laplace transform as a taught topic: transform tables, partial fractions and the inverse transform, solving initial value problems, weight and transfer functions, pole diagrams. Laplace transforms and poles are named in the f.signals summary and converter transfer functions in the pe.modelling summary (and the zh-CN prerequisite path lists the transform for F07), but catalogue.json attaches no lesson or lab to f.signals, and the only transfer-function derivation in the repository is the draft buck tutorial's duty-to-output function.

Bode plots as a taught foundations topic: named in the f.signals summary and the stage-04 outline, tabulated in the draft buck tutorial, but no lesson constructs or reads one (MIT lists a single note, Amplitude Phase, Gain and Bode Plots).

2x2 linear systems: eigenvalues and eigenvectors, normal modes, fundamental matrix, trace-determinant classification of phase portraits, matrix exponential, variation of parameters. The f.linear-algebra summary names state-space descriptions but nothing on eigenvalues; 'eigen', 'phase portrait' and 'matrix exponential' appear in no repository file and f.linear-algebra has no lesson.

Jacobian linearisation of general nonlinear 2x2 systems near critical points, limit cycles and chaos. Linearisation around an operating point is named in the pe.modelling summary (and the pe.modelling mapping above relies on it), but the qualitative theory of nonlinear systems appears nowhere in the repository.

Complex arithmetic, Euler's formula and the complex-exponential method as a self-contained lesson. Complex numbers, phasors and impedance are named in the f.ac summary, the three-phase lesson (curriculum/power-systems/ac-power-networks/three-phase-fundamentals.md) carries a short phasor recap that defers to f.ac, and labs/power-systems/three_phase.py does phasor arithmetic with cmath, but catalogue.json attaches no lesson to f.ac.

courses.coverage_notes: 18.06SC is the OCW Scholar self-study version of MIT's undergraduate linear algebra course (Prof. Gilbert Strang, Fall 2011), organised in three units: (I) solving Ax = b, elimination, LU, inverses and the four fundamental subspaces; (II) orthogonality, projections and least squares, determinants, eigenvalues, diagonalization and the matrix exponential exp(At) for systems of differential equations, Markov matrices and Fourier series; (III) symmetric and positive definite matrices, complex matrices and the FFT, similar matrices and Jordan form, SVD, linear transformations, change of basis and pseudoinverses. Each lecture session pairs a lecture video with a lecture-summary PDF, suggested textbook sections and a recitation (problem-solving) video; 31 of the 36 lecture sessions also carry a problem set with solutions (the overview session, the three exam-review sessions and the final review have none); three unit exams and a final exam with solutions are provided. Applications named on the pages read include electrical networks via incidence matrices, least-squares fitting of data, Markov matrices, Fourier series/FFT and image compression; the course does not treat circuits, converters or power systems as subjects.
gaps: State-space models with inputs and outputs (A, B, C, D matrices), controllability/observability, and state-space averaging of switching converters

Discretisation of a continuous model (Ad = exp(A Ts)), discrete-time state space with inputs, and the z-transform needed for digital control; the course does treat the autonomous recursion u(k+1) = A u(k) in 'Diagonalization and Powers of A'
Laplace transform, transfer functions, poles/zeros and Bode plots linking matrix eigenvalues to frequency response (taught in MIT 18.03 / 6.003, not 18.06)

Numerical linear algebra in practice: floating-point rounding, conditioning, sparse matrices and sparse LU or iterative solvers for large networks, implemented with NumPy/SciPy (the course pages mention only MATLAB and Java demonstrations)
Nonlinear systems: Jacobians and Newton-Raphson iteration (power flow), nonlinear least squares and parameter identification
Recursive least squares and Kalman-type state estimation (grid state estimation, battery state-of-charge estimation)
Three-phase transformations as change of basis: Clarke/Park (dq0) and symmetrical components (Fortescue); the course's change-of-basis and complex-matrix material is not applied to them
Admittance (Ybus) and impedance matrix formulation of AC networks with complex phasor entries
Modal and participation-factor analysis for small-signal stability of converter-dominated grids

Data-driven uses in power and energy (PCA of measurement data, regression on PV/wind resource data): least squares is taught as fitting curves to data (Unit II description) and change of basis is applied to image compression, but neither is applied to power or energy measurement data

Lyapunov energy functions for stability of dynamic systems and quadratic cost functions in control design; the course covers quadratic forms, positive definiteness and minima as mathematics ('Positive Definite Matrices and Minima') without the stability or control application

courses.coverage_notes: MIT 8.02 (Spring 2007) is MIT's first-year electricity-and-magnetism course, the second half of the introductory physics sequence. It is run in the TEAL studio format: short lecture segments alternate with tabletop experiments, electronically polled concept questions and small-group problem work, and one one-hour session a week is given over to problem solving. Its 36 sessions (26 marked Class and 10 marked Problem solving in the Class Topics table) run from electrostatics (charge, field, potential, Gauss's law, conductors and capacitors) through current and DC circuits, magnetostatics (Biot-Savart, Ampere's law, forces and torques on charges, dipoles and current loops), Faraday's law, inductance and transformers, RC/RL/RLC transients and driven AC resonance, to Maxwell's equations, electromagnetic radiation and a closing session on interference. courses.coverage_notes: MIT 6.002 (Spring 2007, Prof. Anant Agarwal; the home page states the course materials were created collaboratively with Prof. Jeffrey H. Lang) is MIT's first undergraduate circuits course, built on the lumped circuit abstraction. Over 25 lectures and 26 recitations it moves from resistive network analysis (KVL/KCL, node method, superposition, Thevenin/Norton) through the digital abstraction and MOSFET switch and amplifier models (large- and small-signal), into capacitors, inductors and first- and second-order transients, then sinusoidal steady state, impedance methods and filters, operational-amplifier feedback circuits, and energy and power in digital/CMOS circuits, ending with a lecture on the limits of the lumped abstraction. Five lab assignments (Lab 0 familiarization; Thevenin/Norton equivalents and logic gates; MOSFET amplifiers and first-order circuits; second-order networks; a mixed analog/digital audio playback system), eleven homework sets, two evening quizzes and a final accompany the lectures. The required textbook is Agarwal and Lang's Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits (title recorded only).

courses.coverage_notes: MIT 6.003 Signals and Systems (Fall 2011, undergraduate, Prof. Dennis Freeman) is a one-semester course in signal and LTI-system analysis that develops the discrete-time and continuous-time cases side by side. The syllabus groups the material into two strands: ways of representing signals (singularity functions, complex exponentials, the Fourier, Laplace and Z transforms, and sampling) and ways of representing linear time-invariant systems (block diagrams, difference or differential equations, system functions with their poles and zeros, convolution sums and integrals, and the impulse, step and frequency responses). The 25 lecture titles run from DT and CT systems through the Z and Laplace transforms, convolution, frequency response, Bode plots and feedback/control to the four Fourier representations, sampling and quantization, modulation and an Audio CD capstone; MIT names control, communications and signal processing as application areas. Format stated on the syllabus: two one-hour lectures and two one-hour recitations per week, graded from three midterms (10%, 15%, 20%), a final exam (40%) and homework, participation and other factors (15%). No lecture, reading, supplementary-note or exam title on the pages read mentions power circuits or converters; nothing is asserted about lecture content beyond those titles.

courses.coverage_notes: MIT 6.622 Power Electronics, Spring 2023, is a graduate subject taught by Prof. David Perreault on the modelling, analysis, design and control of switching circuits that convert electrical energy. Its 38 numbered lectures open with rectifiers, load regulation and power factor, continue with a four-lecture DC/DC block (inferred to be the non-isolated converter family, since isolated converters follow the magnetics block), four magnetics lectures, two lectures on isolated DC/DC converters, switching losses and snubbers, and thermal modelling and heat sinking; the second half covers a three-lecture inverter block, switched-mode rectifiers, three-phase systems and three-phase inverters, converter control including current-mode control, EMI filters (including common-mode and differential-mode noise), switched-capacitor converters, soft switching, resonant power conversion with matching networks, and finally gate drive, level shift and layout. Assessment is by 12 problem sets (Problem Set 0 to 11; homework weighted 40%), 10 short assessments issued roughly weekly in place of exams (50%) and a buck-converter design project (10%) whose deliverables are the power stage, input and output filters, device and heatsink selection, passive components and a closed-loop controller. The textbook is Kassakian, Perreault, Verghese and Schlecht, Principles of Power Electronics (Cambridge University Press, 2023), used as a preprint of the second edition and referred to as KPVS.

courses.coverage_notes: MIT 6.334 Power Electronics (Spring 2007, graduate, Prof. David Perreault) is a one-semester graduate course on using electronic circuits for energy conversion and control, worth 6 engineering design points. Its 37 calendar lectures run from analysis methods and rectifier basics (AC-side reactance, power factor and distortion) through DC-DC converters, magnetics, isolated DC/DC converters, DC-AC inverters and PWM, EMI filtering, loss computation and snubbers, soft switching, thermal design and resonant/RF converters, to averaged modelling and control, three-phase (multi-pulse) rectifier systems, practical layout and gate-drive issues, switched-mode rectifiers and a closing design example. Assessment is weekly problem sets (40%), two evening quizzes (50%, no final exam) and a design project (10%); the required text is Kassakian, Schlecht and Verghese, Principles of Power Electronics, and the OCW site publishes lecture notes and problem sets but no videos.
gaps: Wide-bandgap devices (SiC MOSFETs, GaN HEMTs), their figures of merit, fast-edge gate-drive and dv/dt considerations (pe.devices, pe.gate-driving).
Digital control implementation: sampling, discretisation, PWM resolution, microcontroller/DSP compensators (pe.control).

Bidirectional and dual-active-bridge isolated converters as a taught topology (pe.isolated): no lecture or chapter title names a bidirectional or dual-active-bridge converter; Lec 36 'New topologies' is unspecified, and the home-page image caption mentions a bidirectional automotive DC/DC converter only as an illustration.
Grid-connected converter control: synchronisation/PLL, current control in rotating frames, grid codes, anti-islanding (ps.grid-converters).
Grid-forming converters, inverter-dominated grids and converter-interaction stability (ps.converter-dominated) - not listed on any 6.334 page and must not be attributed to this course.
Open-source simulation workflow (Python, ngspice) replacing the PSpice/PSIM-era tooling on the related-resources page (pe.simulation).
Renewable-energy and storage interfaces: PV maximum power point tracking converters, battery charging and bidirectional storage converters (re.mppt, re.storage, re.pv-systems).
Modern bridgeless/totem-pole power-factor-correction stages with wide-bandgap devices (pe.rectifiers); only 'Switched mode rectifiers' / 'Switching-mode rectifiers' is listed.

EMC standards and pre-compliance measurement practice (CISPR/IEC limits) alongside filter design (pe.emi-pcb): no title names EMC standards or limits; Lec 17 'Intro to EMI' is unspecified and may touch conducted-EMI limits.
Datasheet-driven loss measurement methods such as double-pulse testing and calorimetric efficiency measurement (pe.losses).
Reliability, lifetime and thermal-cycling considerations in converter design (pe.thermal, pe.practical).
Wireless power transfer and modern resonant/high-frequency applications beyond RF amplifiers (pe.resonant, pe.applications).
access_limitations: No lecture videos: the course lists only Lecture Notes and Problem Sets as learning-resource types, so there is no video gallery to cite.

The lecture-notes page lists 16 chapter PDFs that do not map one-to-one onto the 37 calendar lectures (chapter numbering differs from lecture numbering). Only 8 chapter titles are included in topic_outline because of the 45-item cap; the other 8 closely parallel calendar lecture titles and are: ch. 1 Introduction and analysis methods, ch. 3 Power factor and measures of distortion, ch. 5 Introduction to DC/DC converters, ch. 6 Introduction to magnetics, ch. 7 Isolated DC/DC converters, ch. 9 Inverters (DC/AC converters), ch. 12 Soft-switching techniques, ch. 15 Three-phase systems (all read on the lecture-notes page). mapped_modules.mit_topics may cite these chapters although they fall outside topic_outline; each such item carries the [lecture-notes] page tag.

No design-project page or project description is published; the project is known only from the syllabus grading table (10%, issued early April, due Lec 37) and the calendar key dates (project out at Lec 21, due at Lec 37).
Lecture 27 is listed only as 'Guest lecture' with no topic title.

Lecture-note PDFs, the 11 problem-set PDFs, the .LIB/.SLB/.CIR example files and the whole-course download were not opened, in line with the metadata-only rule; coverage judgements rest on page-level titles only.

The related-resources page names proprietary or external tools (PSpice/OrCAD, PSIM demo, LTspice/SwitcherCAD III, a Microsim DesignLab Release 8 evaluation download) and an external SMPS design database; only OrCAD, Powersim and a university SPICE tutorial are hyperlinked, LTspice, the DesignLab download and the database are text mentions, and none of the external sites or files were fetched or checked for current availability.

The course dates from 2007; four of its five listed books are 1990s editions (1991-1998) and the SPICE reference is a 2006 edition. The AIPE catalogue ranks the course 'historical' behind MIT 6.622 (Spring 2023), so it should not be used as evidence for post-2007 practice.

Title conventions in topic_outline and mit_topics: where the calendar shows a unit heading plus a sub-topic line, the record joins them with a colon after the unit number; OCW's parenthetical expansions of abbreviations (LC, CSI, VSI, PWM, EMI, RF, LLC) are dropped from every title for consistency and the 12-word cap, while the parenthetical in Notes ch. 9 'Inverters (DC/AC converters)' is kept because it is part of the chapter title; Lec 17 joins two separate heading blocks on the page (DC-AC Converters 3 and EMI Filters 1). Decomposition of power factor into distortion factor and displacement factor, and THD as a defined metric (Lec 4, Notes ch. 3); pe.rectifiers and ps.three-phase name harmonics and power factor but not these metrics.

Thyristors (SCRs) as power devices and phase-control operation (Notes ch. 4): pe.devices lists diodes, MOSFETs, IGBTs, SiC and GaN but no thyristor, and pe.rectifiers names 'controlled rectifiers' without a lesson for them (see recommended_lessons).
Multi-pulse three-phase rectifiers: six-pulse and twelve-pulse schemes with phase-shifting transformer connections and interphase transformers (Lec 32-33).
Multiple-output isolated converters and the effect of leakage inductance on their regulation (Lec 14).
Multi-winding transformer modelling and high-frequency winding effects in magnetics (Lec 11-12; skin and proximity effects are inferred from the title 'Losses and high-frequency effects', not named).

Current-source versus voltage-source inverters, selective harmonic elimination, harmonic cancellation and multilevel waveform synthesis (Lec 15-16); AIPE's pe.inverters summary stops at bridges, PWM and filters.
EMI filter damping and the interaction of an input filter with converter control (Lec 18 'Damping; Control impact').
Snubber design and diode reverse-recovery effects (Lec 20-21, Notes ch. 11); AIPE's pe.losses summary does not mention snubbers.
Matching networks and RF power circuits as an extension of resonant conversion (Lec 26, Notes ch. 16).

Fourier-series decomposition of switching waveforms as an explicit analysis tool (Lec 15 'Fourier'); pe.rectifiers and pe.inverters name 'harmonics' but no AIPE foundation module summary names Fourier series.

courses.coverage_notes: MIT presents 6.012 Microelectronic Devices and Circuits (Fall 2005, undergraduate, Prof. Jesús del Alamo) as the entry course for its EECS devices/circuits/systems concentration. It starts from semiconductor carrier physics (electron and hole populations, doping with donors and acceptors, drift and diffusion), builds the electrostatics of p-n junctions and MOS structures, derives MOSFET current-voltage characteristics and equivalent-circuit (large-signal and small-signal) models, then applies them to NMOS/CMOS inverter logic (transfer characteristics, delay, scaling, dynamic power). A second device block covers p-n diode I-V, charge storage and diffusion capacitance, and the bipolar junction transistor; the final block treats MOSFET and BJT single-stage and multistage amplifiers, current sources and sinks, and amplifier frequency response (Miller effect, open-circuit time constants). Assessment consists of ten problem sets (the tenth is marked optional on the calendar), two quizzes, a final exam and a SPICE/Cadence circuit design project (an optical receiver). Readings are assigned from the Howe and Sodini textbook for lectures L1-L25.

courses.coverage_notes: MIT 6.302 Feedback Systems (Spring 2007, listed by OCW as Graduate; instructors James Roberge, Joel Dawson, Kent Lundberg) is an introductory feedback-control design course that this record characterises as classical and continuous-time (the record's own terms; no OCW page uses either). Judging from the session titles, it moves from the properties of feedback (desensitivity, linearisation), plant modelling and first/second-order dynamics, through stability tools (root locus, Nyquist criterion, Hall/Nichols charts, Bode gain and phase margins) to compensation design (lead/lag series compensation, minor-loop compensation, internal and external op-amp compensation, lightly damped plants) and finally nonlinear topics (describing functions, oscillators, conditional stability). Physical applications run through a servomotor laboratory (Lab 1A-1D) and a design project chosen from three options (Phase Locked Loop, Thermal-Control System, Magnetic Levitator). The course description's topic list closes with the quoted phrase 'modeling and compensation of power converter systems, and phase lock loops' (11 words, quoted from the home and syllabus pages), although no calendar session title mentions converters explicitly.
gaps: Digital control of converters: sampling, z-domain compensators, ADC and PWM quantisation, computational and PWM delay, anti-windup and firmware implementation (AIPE pe.control 'digital implementation').

Averaged and small-signal modelling of switching converters (state-space averaging, PWM-switch model), control-to-output and line-to-output transfer functions, output impedance, and the right-half-plane zero of boost/buck-boost stages (AIPE pe.modelling, pe.boost) - only named generically in the course description phrase 'modeling and compensation of power converter systems'; whether the unpublished lectures go further is unknown.

Current-mode control specifics: peak and average current-mode control, slope compensation, sampled-data current-loop effects; Type II/Type III compensator design and realisation in converter controller ICs.

Grid-connected converter control: dq-frame current control, synchronous-reference-frame PLLs for three-phase grids, grid-code requirements, grid-support functions (AIPE ps.grid-converters, re.integration).

Impedance-based stability of interconnected converters (Middlebrook input-filter criterion, source-load impedance ratio), small-signal stability of converter-dominated grids, grid-forming and droop control (AIPE ps.converter-dominated, ps.microgrids).

Python-based control tool chain (scipy.signal / python-control) and SPICE-level loop verification with ngspice. The course uses MATLAB and Octave for problem sets (Octave is itself open-source software, so the gap is the specific Python/ngspice chain, not open-source tooling as such) plus Java applets written for Java Plug-in 1.4, which are unlikely to run in current browsers (inference).

Loop-gain measurement of switching converters by injection (Middlebrook/Tian methods, frequency-response analyser) and hardware-in-the-loop verification. Caveat: the course has four hands-on motor labs (1A-1D) and R22 'Return ratio', whose handouts were not read, so general loop-measurement practice may well be covered; only the converter-specific methods are asserted as absent.

State-space and observer-based design, model predictive control and MPPT-style search controllers used in renewable interfaces (AIPE f.linear-algebra, re.mppt); judging from the titles the course is purely classical transfer-function control.
Wide-bandgap-era bandwidth constraints (high switching frequency, EMI filter interaction with control loops) - not attributable to a 2007 classical control course.

concepts_missing_in_aipe: Root locus method (Evans' rules) for seeing how closed-loop poles move with gain or compensator parameters (L7, R7-R8); AIPE lists only Bode-margin thinking.
Nyquist stability criterion and its examples, including conditional stability and gain-window stability (L9, L10, L23, R9-R10).
Degree-of-stability measures beyond phase margin: Hall and Nichols charts, closed-loop peaking M-circles, gain setting from the open-loop plot (L11).
Steady-state error analysis and system type / error constants (L5, R6).
Properties of feedback stated quantitatively: desensitivity, linearisation via feedback, Black's formula, return ratio and loop-gain measurement concepts (L2, R17, R22).

The explicit procedure for turning closed-loop regulation, bandwidth and noise specifications into open-loop Bode constraints (L13-L14, R14-R15); AIPE's pe.control summary lists loop design, but no lesson teaches this specification-to-loop-shape step.

Minor-loop (inner-loop) compensation as a general technique and its relation to series compensation (L17-L18, R18-R20); AIPE mentions current-mode control but has no lesson on the minor-loop principle.

Operational amplifier circuits as feedback systems, analog computers, and internal/external op-amp compensation (R5, L16, L18, L19). AIPE has no op-amp circuit lesson: the taxonomy summary of f.electronics names only diodes and MOSFETs, op-amps appear only as a keyword in the README row for legacy module F06, and the buck tutorial (curriculum/03-converters/buck-converter.md) names the error-amplifier and compensation-network blocks without analysing them.

Describing-function analysis of nonlinear loops, limit cycles and intentional oscillators (L21, L22, R24, Describing Functions Demo) - directly relevant to hysteretic/bang-bang converter control and PWM saturation, absent from AIPE.
Nonlinear compensation for conditionally stable loops (L23).
Time delays in feedback loops and their phase cost (R23) - the foundation for digital-control delay budgeting in pe.control.

Compensating lightly damped quadratic (resonant) plants as a general method (L20). AIPE's buck tutorial already quantifies the LC resonant peak (f0 about 1.3 kHz, Q about 3.9, about 39 dB) and prescribes Type III compensation to cross above it, but there is no general lesson on lightly damped plants beyond that single buck example.

The phase-locked loop analysed as a generic feedback system (linearised phase-detector/loop-filter/VCO model, loop-filter design, lock-in and hold range; R11, R12, Lab 2 option 'Phase Locked Loop'). AIPE's ps.grid-converters names synchronisation, but no module treats PLL loop dynamics as such.

Non-converter physical plants as feedback case studies: servomotor position/velocity control (Lab 1), inverted pendulum (L8), thermal-control system and magnetic levitation (Lab 2 options; the levitator is an unstable plant, inference from the physics).

A hands-on feedback laboratory sequence with a motor mechanism, prelabs and a take-home quiz (Lab 1). AIPE currently has only software-only Python labs (labs/buck_open.py ideal CCM calculation, labs/foundations/dc_circuits.py, labs/power-electronics/buck_switching.py time-domain switching simulation, labs/power-systems/three_phase.py, labs/renewable-energy/pv_model.py); none closes a feedback loop and there is no hardware lab (the buck tutorial's bench section describes an intended comparison that no lesson has yet carried out).

courses.coverage_notes: MIT 6.061 (with a graduate variant 6.690) is an advanced-undergraduate (OCW level: Undergraduate) introduction to electric power systems and electromechanical energy conversion, taught by Prof. James L. Kirtley Jr. in Spring 2011 with two 1.5-hour lectures per week. The 23-lecture calendar starts with a review of network theory, first-order transients (using buck and boost converters as examples) and sinusoidal steady state, then covers transmission lines, polyphase circuits, transformers and per-unit, symmetrical components, faults, protection, phase control and HVDC, and load flow. The second half turns to electromechanics (forces, virtual work) and synchronous, induction, DC and permanent-magnet machines including drive control, and closes with switching power-electronic circuits and inverters. Published materials are a 12-chapter set of course notes labelled '2007 Course Notes' (11 chapter PDFs; chapter 7 not available on OCW), also offered as a single open-textbook PDF, plus 11 problem sets with solutions, one small load-flow program file with problem set 7, and 2 quizzes with solutions; the syllabus names the instructor's Wiley textbook as the text.

courses.coverage_notes: MIT 6.691 (Spring 2006, graduate, Prof. James L. Kirtley Jr.) is a seminar on how bulk electric power systems are planned and operated, taught mainly from an engineering viewpoint with some attention to the economics of a restructured industry. Its self-described 'straw man' calendar runs from a review of complex power and polyphase systems through transmission-line two-port models and sending/receiving-end circle diagrams, transformers, Newton-Raphson and decoupled load flow, synchronous-machine modelling and per-unit models, electromechanical dynamics, voltage regulators and power system stabilizers, small-signal behaviour, generation costs and economic/optimal dispatch, symmetrical components, fault modelling and relaying. The home-page course description (the only fetched page that carries the 'core topics' list) additionally names, as core themes, system protection, multimachine dynamics and control, stability in both its steady-state and transient senses, isolated and mobile power systems, and computation together with simulation; the syllabus page has its own, shorter description, which says the 2006 offering expected to look at DC distribution systems and perhaps renewable sources. Assessment: seven published problem sets with solutions (many problems drawn from the Bergen & Vittal text), two quizzes planned in the straw-man calendar (Q1, Q2; the syllabus says 'perhaps two quizzes' and no quiz materials are published), no final exam, and a term project written at the scale of a conference paper and presented in class. Two sample project reports and two MATLAB simulation scripts are published; there are no lecture videos.
gaps: Grid-connected converter modelling and control: synchronisation (PLL), current control and grid-support functions (ps.grid-converters).
Inverter-dominated and low-inertia grids, grid-forming converters and converter-interaction stability (ps.converter-dominated); the course's stability content is purely synchronous-machine based.
Fault behaviour and protection of converter-fed networks, including limited fault current and inverter-based-resource ride-through (the converter part of ps.protection).

Grid integration of variable renewable generation: variability, grid codes, hosting capacity (re.integration); the syllabus only says renewable sources might perhaps be discussed and no session is listed.
Energy storage in system operation and frequency support (re.storage, re.batteries).
Microgrid droop control, power sharing and energy management, and DC distribution beyond the syllabus's one-sentence mention (ps.microgrids, ps.dc-grids).
HVDC and solid-state transformer interfaces between AC and DC networks (ps.dc-grids, ps.sst).

Dispatch and unit scheduling with variable renewables and storage, and stochastic, forecast-driven scheduling (re.energy-management, ps.grid-control). Security-constrained economic dispatch and locational pricing are not listed as gaps: they may have been touched in L16 'Optimal Dispatch' and the deregulation discussion, and lecture content was not read.
Wide-area measurement (PMU) based monitoring and modern protection schemes (ps.protection, ps.grid-control).

courses.coverage_notes: A graduate course on electromechanics that uses electric machinery as its running example. It starts from field- and energy-based force calculation and magnetic circuits, then covers windings and air-gap fields and the major machine classes: round-rotor and two-reaction (Park transform) synchronous machines with their dynamics and simulation, induction machines (transformer model, squirrel-cage, drives and control, doubly-fed, single-phase, linear), DC commutator machines, variable-reluctance machines and permanent-magnet brushless DC motors, plus transformers, per-unit normalisation, machine sizing and power density, and design evaluation. The stated approach is deliberately classical and analytical, using numerical methods only when necessary; students are expected to be able to design the main classes of rotating and linear machines and to estimate their dynamic parameters. Research-motivated examples named on the syllabus are doubly-fed induction machines (wind turbines, microgrids, ship propulsion) and induction motors for traction drives.

courses.coverage_notes: MIT 2.627 Fundamentals of Photovoltaics (Fall 2013; the OCW data.json also records the companion number 2.626, which no fetched HTML page shows) is an elective in MIT's undergraduate Energy Studies Minor covering the physics of photovoltaic conversion, how cells are made and evaluated, and the market and policy context in which PV technologies compete. The Fall 2013 calendar has 26 sessions in three units: Unit 1 device fundamentals (solar resource, light management, charge excitation, separation, transport and collection, a 1D device model, materials properties), Unit 2 commercial and emerging technologies (wafer silicon, thin films, efficiency limits, emerging concepts, a Fraunhofer CSE field trip), and Unit 3 cross-cutting themes (efficiency-loss troubleshooting; cost and manufacturability with an industry guest lecture on silicon cell manufacturing costs; modules, systems and reliability; price, markets and subsidies; a DOE SunShot guest lecture; PV innovation; PV in developing countries). Lectures 2-12 ran as a flipped classroom using Fall 2011 lecture videos. Hands-on elements are an Arduino-sourcemeter I-V measurement lab, a manufacturing-line simulation assignment using external Virtual MES software, and a team project that weighs technology, economics, policy and social aspects.
gaps: PV inverters and DC-DC stages: MPPT algorithms, string, central and micro-inverter and power-optimizer architectures (no fetched page names MPP, MPPT, a converter or an inverter).
Grid-connected PV behaviour: anti-islanding, grid codes, reactive-power and ride-through requirements, inverter-based-resource stability (the word grid appears on no fetched page).

Post-2013 cell and module technologies and their commercial status: PERC, TOPCon, silicon heterojunction and bifacial modules, and the commercial maturity of perovskite-silicon tandems. The course covers perovskites only as two 2013 student project topics, and treats organics and multijunction devices (lecture-note deck of that title) and emerging or advanced concepts (Lec 15, 2011 video L15) at 2011-2013 depth.
PV combined with storage, hybrid systems, forecasting and energy management (no storage or forecasting title is listed).

Scriptable open-source PV system modelling: pvlib-style irradiance transposition, module temperature models, performance ratio and degradation analysis from field data, plus post-2013 LCOE and cost data. The course's Session 2 PVWatts Calculator activity is a PV-system yield model, and its cost and market data are 2011-2013 vintage.

System-level safety and reliability practice as it stands today: arc-fault and rapid-shutdown requirements, potential-induced degradation and soiling analytics with modern field data. The course's Lec 19 covers module and system reliability at 2011-2013 level.

courses.coverage_notes: EC.S07 (Edgerton Center, Fall 2004, undergraduate, Prof. Louis Bucciarelli) is a one-session-per-week, two-hour class (the syllabus labels the meetings 'Lectures') on the behaviour and first-order conceptual design of photovoltaic systems, with the emphasis on stand-alone (off-grid) PV-plus-battery systems for any location in the US. The 14-session calendar moves from the solar resource (sun geometry, clearness index, US insolation databases and TMY data) through module I-V behaviour and array networking to stand-alone system elements, three sessions of stand-alone sizing (first-order estimation of average daily performance, then loss-of-load probability with a Markov process model and the effect of day-to-day correlation), evaluation of PV station data, two sessions on grid-connected systems (power conditioning, utility constraints, architectural/structural considerations) and cost/benefit analysis with net present value and government incentives. Assessment is a semester-long project built from five exercises and a final report; no final exam is given. Hardware is treated only at an introductory level, as the course description states.

courses.coverage_notes: MIT 8.21 The Physics of Energy (Physics Department, Fall 2009, undergraduate; instructors listed as Prof. Robert Jaffe and Prof. Washington Taylor) is a quantitative physics course on energy for students who already have introductory physics, calculus and chemistry: it asks where energy comes from, how it is extracted, moved, stored, lost and finally used, and which physical laws limit each step. Part I (Energy and its Uses) covers energy units and scales, mechanical, thermal and electromagnetic energy, an introduction to quantum energy levels, chemical energy and CO2 flows, entropy and temperature, heat engines, phase-change conversion with refrigeration and heat pumps, internal combustion engines, and steam and gas power cycles. Part II (Sources of Energy) covers fundamental forces, quantum mechanics for nuclear physics, nuclear forces and binding energy, fusion, fission and fission-reactor physics, design and safety, the flow of energy in the universe, solar radiation, solar-thermal and photovoltaic conversion, biological and fossil fuels, wind resource and turbine physics, geothermal and ocean-thermal energy, and tidal, wave and hydro power. Part III (Systems and Synthesis) covers nuclear radiation, fuel cycles, waste and proliferation, climate change (three sessions), energy storage and energy conservation. The syllabus presents it as a quantitative course rather than a survey; political, economic, social and ethical issues are not discussed directly (the syllabus says the course supplies the scientific foundation for evaluating them).

courses.coverage_notes: MIT 10.626 Electrochemical Energy Systems, Spring 2014, Prof. Martin Bazant, Department of Chemical Engineering, graduate level. The Instructor Insights page states that the class contains both graduate and undergraduate students and that students taking the graduate version complete additional assignments; the course number 10.426 appears only in the course's data.json as recorded in references/mit-ocw-verification.json (observed.extra_course_numbers), not on any of the eight fetched HTML pages. The course teaches the physics and mathematical modelling of electrochemical energy conversion and storage in five parts: I Introduction (galvanic cells, conversion, storage), II Circuit Models (equivalent-circuit dynamics and impedance), III Thermodynamics (statistical thermodynamics and solution models, Nernst equation and open-circuit voltage, Pourbaix diagrams, metal-acid and Li-ion cells, pseudocapacitance, phase separation), IV Kinetics (Faradaic reactions, Butler-Volmer equation, electrocatalysis, electrochemical phase transformations, charge-transfer theory) and V Transport Phenomena (concentration polarization, transient diffusion, Warburg impedance, forced convection, transport in solids and bulk electrolytes, double layers, porous media, scaling analysis, porous electrodes). Applications named on the pages are batteries, fuel cells, supercapacitors and electrokinetics. Inference from the session titles only: no session title mentions power-electronic interfaces, battery management systems or grid-level storage operation; the pages make no statement about these topics.
gaps: Battery management systems: cell voltage/temperature monitoring, passive and active balancing, protection, and state-of-charge / state-of-health estimation algorithms (Coulomb counting, model-based observers) built on equivalent-circuit models.
Battery ageing and degradation (calendar and cycle ageing, SEI growth, lithium plating), thermal runaway and safety engineering - no session title on ageing or safety.
Pack-level engineering: series/parallel configuration, cell-to-pack, thermal management, contactors and pre-charge, fusing and isolation.
Power-electronic interfaces for storage: bidirectional DC/DC stages, grid-tied inverters, CC-CV and fast-charging profiles, charger topologies.

Grid-scale storage roles and system metrics: frequency regulation, arbitrage, capacity firming, system round-trip efficiency, levelised cost of storage, and comparison with non-electrochemical storage (pumped hydro, flywheels, thermal, hydrogen).
Post-2014 chemistries and formats: high-nickel NMC/NCA, LFP at pack level, sodium-ion, silicon anodes, solid-state electrolytes - only Li-ion and metal-acid cells are listed.

Engineering-level battery test methods: capacity and C-rate tests, HPPC-type pulse tests for internal resistance, cycle-life testing and datasheet reading. The course does cover laboratory electroanalytical characterisation (electrochemical impedance, sessions 5-7 and 27; linear sweep voltammetry, session 14), so the gap is the engineering test protocols, not characterisation as such.
Hydrogen and fuel-cell system integration (electrolysers, fuel-cell stacks with power electronics) beyond the electrochemistry of the cell.

Open-source simulation tooling for storage (Python equivalent-circuit model fitting, physics-based battery model packages) and reproducible labs - the course has no computational component visible on its pages.
Second-life use, recycling, sustainability and standards/grid-code requirements for stationary storage.

concepts_missing_in_aipe: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and equivalent-circuit elements of a cell (series resistance, charge-transfer resistance, double-layer capacitance, Warburg/diffusion impedance) - AIPE's f.ac covers impedance only for ideal R, L and C elements (ps.per-unit uses per-unit impedances) and no lesson covers cell impedance.
Nernst equation and open-circuit voltage as a function of composition - the physical basis of OCV versus state-of-charge curves - is not named in any AIPE module summary or lesson.
Pourbaix diagrams and electrochemical stability windows (electrolyte and electrode stability, corrosion) - no AIPE coverage.
Activation overpotential and Butler-Volmer / Tafel kinetics, exchange current density and electrocatalysis - no AIPE coverage.
Concentration polarization, diffusion limitation and limiting current as the origin of rate capability and capacity fade at high C-rate - no AIPE coverage.

Fuel cells (thermodynamic voltage, polarization curve, transport losses) - fuel cells, electrolysers and hydrogen storage appear in no AIPE module summary at all, a module-level gap in the energy-storage and energy-conversion tracks.

Supercapacitors: double-layer capacitance, pseudocapacitance and porous-electrode (RC-ladder) behaviour - re.storage names 'storage technologies' generally but no lesson or sub-module treats supercapacitors.

Phase-separating intercalation electrodes and electrochemical phase transformations (why some Li-ion chemistries have flat voltage plateaus) - graduate-level; an advanced sidebar candidate for re.batteries.
Porous electrode theory and scaling analysis of energy versus power (Ragone-type reasoning from first principles) - AIPE has 'energy and power ratings' but not the physics behind them.

Solution thermodynamics (ideal and regular solution models, statistical thermodynamics) (the energy-conversion track summary names physical and thermodynamic foundations generally, but no module summary names solution models or statistical thermodynamics), linear sweep voltammetry, homogeneous/heterogeneous charge-transfer theory, forced convection in electrochemical cells, electrokinetics and quantum theory of electrodes - chemical-engineering depth that is outside AIPE's electrical-engineering scope and should stay as 'further reading' only.

courses.coverage_notes: An undergraduate social-science survey course (Sloan School of Management, jointly offered with Economics, Anthropology, and Urban Studies and Planning; the OCW HTML pages show only the number 15.031J, while the project's verification record lists the additional numbers 14.43J, 21A.341J and 11.161J taken from the course data.json; a core subject of MIT's Energy Studies Minor) on how energy choices are made at every level from the individual household up to firms, movements and governments, drawing on economics, management, political science, sociology and anthropology. Six units run from an overview of the U.S. and comparative energy systems, through the climate problem (including a simulation-based negotiation role play), household and business decision-making (energy demand economics, financial and normative frameworks, cases on combined heat and power and biodiesel, strategy and business models), primary energy and the electric power system (non-renewable resources, shale, today's and tomorrow's grid), to public-policy processes and team paper presentations. Judging from session and reading titles (slides and videos were not opened), it is not an engineering course: no circuit, converter, machine or power-flow topics are listed; its relevance to AIPE is the economics, markets, resources and policy context of energy systems.
